what: Whether a cheating node can be named from what the protocol already sends, predicted before the decoder was written
the_current_answer: No. Protocols/MaliciousShamirMC.hpp reconstructs from t+1 shares, reconstructs again from every longer prefix, and on disagreement throws mac_fail('inconsistent Shamir secret sharing'). The string contains no party index and none is computed.
why_it_could_be_yes: Shamir shares of a degree-t secret are a Reed-Solomon codeword RS[n, t+1]. At n=7, t=2 that is RS[7,3], minimum distance 5, so Berlekamp-Welch corrects floor((5-1)/2) = 2 errors --- exactly T --- and returns the error locator polynomial, whose roots are the evaluation points of the parties that sent wrong shares. The information is in the data the protocol already moves; nothing extra has to be sent.

predictions.quantity: how many wrong shares can be located at n=7, t=2, degree-t sharings
predictions.falsifiable: locating 3, or failing at 2, refutes the RS parameters

predictions.quantity: how many at degree-2t (a product before degree reduction)
predictions.consequence: so the guarantee is T on ordinary values and T-1 on unreduced products, which is why a robust protocol has to be designed around it rather than just decoding harder

predictions.predicted: under 100 microseconds per decode in CPython
predictions.arithmetic: one n x n linear solve over the field, n = 7, so a few hundred field operations

predictions.predicted: MP-SPDZ collects 2t+1 = 5 shares for a public opening. RS[5,3] has distance 3 and corrects one error, not two. Locating T = 2 needs all seven shares, so n instead of 2t+1: 40 percent more per opening.

predictions.quantity: THE LIMIT THAT MATTERS. does this locate a node that substituted its INPUT?
predictions.predicted: NO, and this is the important half of the answer.
predictions.why: secret_input() sums one additive share per party. A substituted input is a valid sharing of a different value --- there is no inconsistency, so there is no error to locate. Decoding answers 'who sent a malformed share', not 'who lied about their value'. Those are different questions and only the first is free.

predictions.quantity: what locating a substituted input would take
predictions.predicted: n openings instead of 1, and n masks instead of 1
predictions.how: the input check opens one combination over all inputs. Opening one combination per PARTY --- over only that party's contributions, each under its own mask --- names the party. The masks are the expensive part: they are what forced the 164-bit field in the first place.
